```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`misskappa` estimates weighted agreement coefficients (Conger, Fleiss,
Brennan–Prediger) when some ratings are **missing**, with standard errors,
confidence intervals, and equality tests.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(misskappa)
```

## A first agreement coefficient

`dat.gwet2014` is a small rating matrix (20 subjects, five raters, four
ordered categories) with some ratings missing (`NA`). The default estimator,
inverse-probability weighting (`"ipw"`), is consistent when ratings are
missing completely at random (MCAR) and is the recommended starting point:

```{r}
#| warning: false
fit <- agreement(dat.gwet2014, weight = "linear")
fit
```

Ratings can be numbers, strings, or factors. `categories = 0:4` would declare
a fifth, unused category, which changes Brennan–Prediger and the linear
weights. The print method shows each coefficient with its standard error and
a 95% confidence interval. The pieces are available directly:

```{r}
coef(fit)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
```

### Confidence intervals

`confint()` gives natural-scale Wald intervals, or a variance-stabilizing
Fisher *z* interval that always stays inside `(-1, 1)`, useful when a
coefficient is close to the boundary:

```{r}
confint(fit)
confint(fit, transform = "fisher")
```

On complete data with few subjects, `confint(fit, method = "jackknife")` gives
exact delete-one jackknife intervals with a *t* critical value instead.
`?confint.misskappa_estimate` lists the fits that support it. For a tidy
summary, `as.data.frame(fit)` returns one row per coefficient with its
estimate, standard error, and interval.

## Choosing an estimator

Start with `"ipw"`. The others suit specific situations:

| Function and data | `estimator` | Assumption |
|---|---|---|
| `agreement()`, categorical ratings | `"ipw"` | MCAR, rater-varying observation rates |
| `agreement()`, categorical ratings | `"cat_fiml"` | Ignorable (MCAR or MAR), saturated multinomial |
| `agreement()`, scored ratings | `"pairwise"` | MCAR, distribution-free, saturated covariance |
| `agreement()`, scored ratings | `"nt_fiml"` | Ignorable, normal-theory, saturated covariance |
| `agreement()`, scored ratings | `"nt_fiml_cs"` | Ignorable, normal-theory, compound-symmetry covariance |
| `agreement_counts()`, category counts | `"fleiss_cuzick"` | MCAR, exchangeable raters |
| `agreement_counts()`, category counts | `"cat_fiml"` | Ignorable, exchangeable raters |
| `agreement_counts()`, category counts | `"nt_fiml_cs"` | Ignorable, exchangeable raters, normal-theory |

Use `"cat_fiml"` when missingness may depend on the observed ratings (MAR)
and there are few raters and categories. The scored estimators treat the
categories as numbers and use the quadratic weight. They report
Brennan–Prediger only when the scale is declared:

```{r}
agreement(dat.zapf2016, estimator = "pairwise")
agreement(dat.zapf2016, estimator = "nt_fiml", categories = 1:5)
```

`"nt_fiml_cs"` assumes compound symmetry, which lets it work on
planned-incomplete designs where some rater pairs never rate the same subject.
The [estimators article](articles/missingness-estimators.html) explains the
trade-offs and works through such a design.

## Counts-format data

When raters are interchangeable and you only have per-subject category counts,
use `agreement_counts()`. `dat.fleiss1971` is the classic psychiatric-diagnosis
table (30 subjects, six raters, five categories):

```{r}
agreement_counts(dat.fleiss1971)
```

`ratings_to_counts()` turns a subjects-by-raters matrix into this format.

## Beyond pairwise agreement

Set `g > 2` for kernels that compare `g` raters at once, or pass a
subjects-by-raters-by-features array for vector-valued ratings. The
[beyond pairwise agreement](articles/beyond-pairwise.html) article covers
both.

## Comparing coefficients

Every fit carries a per-subject influence matrix `fit$psi` with
`vcov == crossprod(psi) / n^2`. That is what a Wald test needs, so
`agreement_test()` compares a coefficient across fits and returns an `htest`.
Only the covariance of the contrast changes between designs:

* **one sample**: the coefficient's own variance
* **independent samples**: the per-fit variances add (block diagonal)
* **paired / same-subject**: the cross-fit dependence is read from the
  stacked influence functions `fit$psi`


### One sample: is a coefficient equal to a fixed value?

Pass a single fit and a `value`. This tests whether the (nominal) Conger
coefficient for the Gwet (2014) data equals 0.5. Conger is the first
coefficient of a `agreement()` fit, so it is the default `coef`:

```{r}
agreement_test(agreement(dat.gwet2014, estimator = "ipw"), value = 0.5)
```

### Independent samples: two studies, different subjects

When the fits come from disjoint sets of subjects the variances add. This is
the default (`paired = FALSE`). Here the Conger coefficient is compared between
the Gwet (2014) and Klein (2018) studies:

```{r}
agreement_test(
  gwet  = agreement(dat.gwet2014,  estimator = "ipw"),
  klein = agreement(dat.klein2018, estimator = "ipw")
)
```

### Paired: same subjects, two coefficients

When both coefficients are computed on the *same* subjects, the two estimates
are correlated and ignoring that dependence gives the wrong standard error.
`paired = TRUE` takes the dependence from the influence functions.

A clean illustration on **real crowdsourced data**: in `dat.mcduff2019`, MTurk
judges rate smiling images on two attributes (*smile presence* and *image
positivity*). Each image is rated on a 1-6 scale by only a handful of the 121
judges, and almost no two judges share images, so the judges are treated as
exchangeable and each image is summarised by its category counts. Because both
coefficients are estimated on the same items, the contrast is dependent.

```{r}
to_counts <- function(attribute) {
  m <- with(dat.mcduff2019,
            tapply(get(attribute), list(item, judge), function(z) z[1]))
  ratings_to_counts(matrix(as.numeric(m), nrow = nrow(m)))
}
smile    <- agreement_counts(to_counts("rating_smile"),    weight = "quadratic")
positive <- agreement_counts(to_counts("rating_positive"), weight = "quadratic")

agreement_test(smile = smile, positive = positive, paired = TRUE)
```

### *G*-way homogeneity: are several coefficients all equal?

With more than two fits the test becomes the joint hypothesis that they are all
equal, with `G - 1` degrees of freedom.

Is the two-rater quadratic coefficient constant across all rater pairs? The
Zapf (2016) data has four raters and hence six pairs, all on the same 50
subjects:

```{r}
pairs <- combn(4, 2)
pair_fits <- apply(pairs, 2, function(rs)
  agreement(dat.zapf2016[, rs], estimator = "pairwise"), simplify = FALSE)
names(pair_fits) <- apply(pairs, 2, paste0, collapse = "")
do.call(agreement_test, c(pair_fits, list(paired = TRUE)))
```

### Custom contrasts

`agreement_test()` covers equality of one coefficient. For anything else,
build the test from the influence rows: a linear contrast of coefficients has
influence function equal to the same linear combination of the columns of
`psi` (`stats::influence(fit)` returns the same matrix). Are Conger and
Brennan-Prediger equal within one fit?

```{r}
fit <- agreement(dat.tenhove2025, estimator = "nt_fiml_cs", categories = 1:5)
psi <- influence(fit)
est <- coef(fit)[["Conger"]] - coef(fit)[["Brennan-Prediger"]]
se  <- sqrt(sum((psi[, "Conger"] - psi[, "Brennan-Prediger"])^2)) / nrow(psi)
c(estimate = est, se = se, z = est / se)
```

For fits on the same subjects, subtract their influence columns row by row in
the same way; the rows are named by subject.
